faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a system of two stars orbiting each other in a plane that lines up with our view from Earth. As they orbit, one star periodically passes in front of the other, blocking some of its light. This creates a regular dip in the total brightness we observe - a pattern that repeats with the orbital period. By studying these light dips, astronomers can measure the orbital period and learn about the relative sizes and brightnesses of the two stars.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?

faqs.answer: 'Candidate' means the automated pipeline found a pattern in the light curve consistent with an eclipsing binary. 'Confirmed' on Star Vetter means the candidate passed an automated pixel-level check - a test that verifies the brightness dips are coming from the target star itself, not from a nearby star that happened to be blended into the same pixel. Confirmation by this pipeline does not mean the object has been independently verified or published in the scientific literature; it is simply the project's own vetting gate.
faqs.question: What does 'candidate' mean, and how is it different from 'confirmed' on this site?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter includes a machine-learning model (histogram gradient boosting) trained on over 3,100 labeled examples. It provides a second opinion on candidate quality and performs better than the rule-based baseline used in the pipeline. However, the ML score is not currently used to decide which candidates undergo pixel-level checking. All candidates that pass statistical vetting and the novelty cross-check proceed to the pixel check regardless of their ML score. The model offers independent confidence information but does not gate or filter the vetting process.
faqs.question: What is the machine-learning screening score?

faqs.answer: After statistical vetting and cross-checking against known catalogs, each candidate undergoes an automated pixel-level check. This test examines the pixel data to confirm that the brightness variations originate from the target star and not from contamination by nearby objects. The pixel check is fully automated - not done by a human - and decides whether a candidate receives the 'confirmed' label on this site.
faqs.question: How does the pipeline check whether a candidate is real?

faqs.answer: Some eclipsing binaries can produce ambiguous patterns in their light curves if they have similar eclipse depths at each orbit. Star Vetter includes an odd/even eclipse-depth test: it compares the brightness dips from odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses to help detect cases where the measured period might be an alias (for instance, half the true period). Candidates flagged by this test are noted on their individual pages so you are aware of the caveat.
faqs.question: What if the orbital period looks aliased?

faqs.answer: Yes. Every confirmed candidate on Star Vetter includes its light curve and basic measured properties - orbital period and relative eclipse depths. You can download the data and examine it yourself. Keep in mind that the pixel-level check has already been performed by the automated pipeline, so you know the target star itself shows the eclipse signature. For a fully independent verification, you would need access to the original TESS data and your own analysis tools.
faqs.question: Can I verify a result myself?

faqs.answer: Being listed on this site represents the end of what the Star Vetter pipeline itself does. The candidate is not automatically added to major astronomical catalogs, has not received professional follow-up, and is not submitted to the scientific literature by this project. Star Vetter makes the results available here for other researchers and the public to find and use. Any further scientific study, confirmation, or publication is beyond the scope of this automated vetting system.
faqs.question: What happens after a candidate is listed on Star Vetter?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. Eclipsing binaries are pairs of stars that orbit each other and periodically block each other's light as seen from Earth, creating a telltale dip in brightness. The pipeline starts with over 21,000 TESS targets, applies statistical quality checks to light curves, cross-references results against six major variable-star catalogs to avoid re-reporting known objects, and then runs an automated pixel-level check to confirm that the brightness dips come from the target star itself rather than nearby objects. So far, this process has confirmed 304 eclipsing binary candidates. A machine-learning model trained on over 3,000 labeled examples provides an independent assessment of candidate quality, outperforming the rule-based baseline. Each confirmed candidate is listed here with its light curve, measured orbital period, and relative eclipse depths - but like any automated pipeline, some candidates may carry open questions noted on their individual pages.
